frictionVectors.title: EU energy leverage
frictionVectors.details: Europe remains dependent on Algerian gas while pressing for greater market flexibility and investment access. Algeria is using long-term contracts and state control of hydrocarbons to preserve bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara and Sahel spillover
frictionVectors.details: Tensions with Morocco and instability across the Sahel constrain regional infrastructure integration. Security priorities also raise the cost of developing southern mineral and energy corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains central to export earnings and fiscal stability, leaving sovereignty exposed to price cycles and international capital. Declining mature fields intensify pressure to attract foreign operators and technology.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure finance
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed rail, energy, and construction networks remain strategically important despite Luanda's efforts to diversify partners. Debt, contract transparency, and repayment capacity continue to shape policy space.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel insecurity reaches the north
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence near the Burkina Faso and Niger borders threatens transport routes, local economies, and state access to resource zones. Security spending is increasing while regional cooperation remains uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Regional trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Cotonou and transit trade remain vulnerable to policy shifts in Nigeria and neighboring Sahel states. Benin is strengthening domestic processing and energy links to reduce exposure to external chokepoints.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains substantial negotiating power through state participation and value-sharing arrangements, but diamond demand and pricing remain externally determined. Synthetic stones and weaker global consumption create strategic pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Water and power constraints
frictionVectors.details: Chronic water scarcity and dependence on regional electricity markets limit industrial diversification. New solar, transmission, and water infrastructure require foreign capital without surrendering policy control.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-sector control and insecurity
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state control over gold production and licensing, but insurgent activity and informal mining reduce effective oversight. Export routes and revenue collection remain vulnerable to armed groups and illicit networks.

frictionVectors.title: Geopolitical realignment
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou has reduced reliance on France and expanded security and political ties with Russia, gaining diplomatic room but not a guaranteed security solution. Sanctions, aid disruption, and weak infrastructure access increase economic costs.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals dependence
frictionVectors.details: Bujumbura is seeking greater state control over nickel, gold, and rare-earth projects, but limited capital and technical capacity leave room for foreign firms to shape contracts and export chains.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border tension
frictionVectors.details: Mutual accusations over armed groups and border insecurity continue to disrupt regional trade and constrain Burundi's access to transport and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Port competition and external leverage
frictionVectors.details: Praia is balancing European, American, Chinese, and regional interest in its ports and maritime facilities while trying to preserve strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing access and limited enforcement capacity create recurring concerns over depleted stocks, licensing transparency, and the distribution of maritime revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed transport and energy projects remain important to Cameroon’s development but increase exposure to debt, procurement, and operating concessions that can dilute state leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone and northern insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest, alongside Boko Haram-linked violence in the Far North, threatens roads, plantations, and cross-border resource flows.

frictionVectors.title: Russian influence over concessions
frictionVectors.details: Russian security networks remain central to regime protection and are widely associated with privileged access to gold and diamond operations, limiting transparent national control.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The landlocked state depends heavily on routes through Cameroon and neighboring states, leaving fuel, trade, and humanitarian access vulnerable to insecurity and external chokepoints.

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chad’s fiscal position remains highly exposed to oil prices, foreign operators, and export infrastructure, constraining efforts to convert resource income into broad sovereign development.

frictionVectors.title: Post-French security realignment
frictionVectors.details: N'Djamena is recalibrating ties after the reduction of French military involvement while managing instability from Sudan, Libya, and armed groups across the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: French Control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France's administration of Mayotte remains the central sovereignty dispute, limiting Comoros' leverage over maritime access, migration, and surrounding resources.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Limited fiscal capacity leaves major transport, energy, and telecommunications projects dependent on foreign financing and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Mining Value Chains
frictionVectors.details: Copper and cobalt production remains exposed to foreign firms, trading networks, and opaque contract structures, while domestic processing capacity lags behind extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda-Linked Conflict Pressures
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to threaten mining corridors and state authority, with regional rivalries and external political support complicating sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Dominance of Hydrocarbons
frictionVectors.details: The economy and public finances remain heavily tied to offshore oil operated through foreign partnerships, leaving limited domestic control over technology, marketing, and downstream value.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Debt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed roads, rail links, and industrial projects expand connectivity but may deepen creditor and contractor dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capture of Agricultural Value
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is seeking greater local processing and producer income, but global firms still retain substantial influence over cocoa financing, logistics, and pricing.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Security Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Militant activity and instability from the Sahel place pressure on border infrastructure and security spending, increasing reliance on external partners.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Foreign Military Presence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through US, Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but the concentration of foreign forces constrains strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Debt Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Port revenues and logistics infrastructure are closely tied to Ethiopia's trade and foreign-financed projects, creating vulnerability to creditor leverage and regional shocks.

highlights: Suez remains a strategic revenue shield

frictionVectors.title: Debt and asset dependence
frictionVectors.details: Large Gulf-backed investments and external financing stabilize Egypt but increase foreign influence over strategic land, ports, and infrastructure. Debt-service pressures constrain independent economic policymaking.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Suez traffic faces disruption from regional conflict, while the Nile dispute with Ethiopia remains unresolved. Both pressures directly affect Egypt's trade revenues and water security.

frictionVectors.title: Declining oil and gas output
frictionVectors.details: Mature fields and weak diversification leave the state dependent on foreign operators, technical expertise, and volatile hydrocarbon revenues. Falling production narrows fiscal room and bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Gas infrastructure concentration
frictionVectors.details: LNG and gas-processing projects remain central to national revenue, but their financing, technology, and market access rely heavily on external partners. This limits fully sovereign control over the energy chain.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold, copper, and zinc operations provide hard currency but are dominated by external capital and technical capacity. Opaque contracts and labor concerns make resource sovereignty a persistent vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea's coastline and proximity to Yemen and the Bab el-Mandeb attract competing regional security interests. Port and basing speculation increases outside pressure while the government resists formal dependence.

highlights: Sugar and forestry anchor export control

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure dependence on South Africa
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini relies heavily on South African roads, ports, electricity links, and customs channels. This creates structural exposure to Pretoria's economic conditions and regional policy choices.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal pressure and external finance
frictionVectors.details: Public finances remain vulnerable to swings in customs revenue, remittances, and agricultural exports. External lenders and investors can gain leverage as the government seeks infrastructure and budget support.

frictionVectors.title: Nile dam diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam expands Ethiopia's control over electricity generation and water infrastructure, but unresolved arrangements with Egypt and Sudan keep regional tensions elevated. External mediation has not produced a durable operating framework.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and financing needs create leverage for international lenders over railways, logistics, telecommunications, and energy policy. The government is seeking greater control while balancing access to foreign capital.

frictionVectors.title: Resource-contract renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The post-transition government is seeking greater domestic value capture from oil, manganese and timber while preserving investor confidence. Contract reviews could strain relations with established French, Chinese and regional operators.

frictionVectors.title: Rail and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Export corridors for manganese and other minerals remain vulnerable to infrastructure bottlenecks and concentrated foreign operating interests. Libreville is balancing Chinese financing and commercial ties with longstanding French influence.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fishing agreements and weak monitoring continue to limit The Gambia's control over marine resources. Illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing threatens coastal livelihoods and state revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Banjul port vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Trade and energy security remain tied to the port, road links and cooperation with Senegal. External financing and logistics dependence constrain Banjul's bargaining power over strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal gold mining
frictionVectors.details: Galamsey continues to damage water systems, farmland and state authority, with networks involving domestic financiers and foreign-linked equipment suppliers. Enforcement is politically costly and complicates efforts to formalize artisanal mining.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and mining leverage
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pushing local processing and tighter participation in lithium and gold value chains while managing fiscal pressure and dependence on external capital. Chinese, Australian and other investors remain important to project development and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou consortium influence
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore and rail-port complex offers historic revenue potential but places Guinea's export infrastructure in the hands of large foreign-led consortia. Concession terms, local processing and revenue transparency remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Transition and resource bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The military government uses mining approvals and bauxite policy to strengthen domestic leverage while facing pressure over the return to civilian rule. Sanctions risk and political uncertainty could affect financing, operations and investor alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew value-chain capture
frictionVectors.details: Dependence on raw cashew exports leaves farmers and public finances exposed to foreign buyers, price swings and limited domestic processing. Attempts to regulate exports and expand local industry repeatedly collide with weak institutions and elite brokerage.

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Bissau's port and coastline remain vulnerable to underinvestment, smuggling and transnational narcotics networks. External partners can provide infrastructure and security support, but political instability limits effective sovereign oversight.

frictionVectors.title: External financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: Debt-service pressures and IMF-linked reforms constrain Nairobi's room to renegotiate major infrastructure and energy commitments involving Chinese, Gulf, and Western lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor competition
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa and the LAPSSET corridor face competition from Tanzanian and Djiboutian routes, while security risks in northern Kenya raise the cost of regional connectivity.

highlights: Water sovereignty tied to South Africa

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project dependence
frictionVectors.details: Revenue and infrastructure from water exports to South Africa remain central to Lesotho's fiscal position, limiting bargaining autonomy and exposing the kingdom to project delays and bilateral pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Textile and infrastructure vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: The economy remains dependent on externally controlled textile supply chains and donor-backed infrastructure, making employment and development vulnerable to shifts in trade preferences.

highlights: Ports and mining attract strategic competition

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession control
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore and other mineral projects bring essential capital but leave Liberia exposed to disputes over concession terms, local content, land rights, and the distribution of royalties.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor influence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and financiers remain important to port modernization and transport links, creating sovereignty concerns whenever infrastructure access is tied to long-term commercial or security interests.

highlights: Oil remains divided among rival authorities

frictionVectors.title: Fragmented oil governance
frictionVectors.details: Competing institutions, armed groups, and regional power centers continue to contest control over production, export terminals, and revenue flows, weakening the National Oil Corporation's effective sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military and energy footholds
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Russia, Gulf actors, and European states retain influence through security partnerships, bases, contractors, and energy interests, limiting Libya's ability to independently manage ports and strategic assets.

highlights: Critical minerals draw intense outside interest
Resource governance struggles to capture value

frictionVectors.title: Mining concession dependence
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, and other mineral projects are dominated by foreign capital and technology, while environmental disputes and limited domestic processing constrain Madagascar's share of the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure-for-access pressure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Gulf, and Western partners compete for influence through ports, roads, energy, and agricultural projects, raising concerns that infrastructure access may outpace regulatory and local-benefit safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-linked reforms limit policy space, while donor and lender support remains essential for imports, energy, and fiscal stability.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals infrastructure gap
frictionVectors.details: Prospective uranium, rare-earth, and niobium projects attract foreign investors, but weak power, rail, and transport infrastructure reduces Malawi's bargaining leverage.

highlights: Junta asserts control over mining rents
Russian security ties deepen strategic dependence

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty confrontation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are pressing foreign miners for larger state shares and tax compliance, increasing disputes with international operators and investors.

frictionVectors.title: Security partnership dependency
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian-linked security personnel and equipment provides regime support but creates new external leverage as insecurity persists across the Sahel.

frictionVectors.title: Gas-sector external dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers major revenue potential, but offshore production, financing, and marketing remain dependent on foreign operators and partners.

frictionVectors.title: Transport and border vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore logistics and planned green-hydrogen infrastructure require substantial external capital, while Sahel instability threatens inland corridors and investor confidence.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos sovereignty transition
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago remains tied to negotiations over the Diego Garcia military facility and the interests of the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean strategic competition
frictionVectors.details: Indian, Chinese, Western, and regional interests compete for maritime, port, and surveillance access, requiring careful balancing by Port Louis.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables reinforce state leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource diplomacy
frictionVectors.details: Control and development of Western Sahara underpin Morocco's strategic position but continue to generate legal, diplomatic, and trade friction with Algeria, the Polisario Front, and some foreign partners.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign capital in strategic infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: European, Gulf, Chinese, and other investors support ports, rail, energy, and automotive supply chains, creating growth while exposing key sectors to external influence.

highlights: LNG Restart Hangs on Cabo Delgado Security
Gas Wealth Constrained by Fiscal and Sovereignty Risks

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado LNG Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent violence and reliance on foreign security support continue to delay major LNG development. International operators retain substantial leverage over project timing, financing, and revenue structures.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Contract Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt pressures and opaque past borrowing limit Maputo's bargaining power with lenders, contractors, and energy companies. LNG expectations remain central to fiscal planning despite uncertain production dates.

highlights: Critical Minerals and Oil Attract Global Competition
Green Hydrogen Ambition Tests Domestic Control

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Resource Licensing
frictionVectors.details: Recent oil discoveries and uranium, lithium, and rare-earth prospects have intensified competition among international firms and state-backed investors. Namibia is seeking local value addition, but capital and technical dependence remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Green Hydrogen Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen projects depend on foreign finance, export infrastructure, and long-term offtake agreements. The government must balance rapid development with land rights, water use, and domestic industrial benefits.

highlights: Junta Reasserts Control over Uranium and Oil
Sanctions and Security Gaps Constrain Sovereignty

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Military authorities are challenging established French-linked mining arrangements while seeking alternative partners. The shift may increase state control but risks reduced investment, technical disruption, and opaque concessions.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Export Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Niger's crude exports rely on cross-border pipeline infrastructure and vulnerable regional transit relationships. Political tensions with coastal neighbors and sanctions increase the risk that foreign or neighboring actors control access to revenue.

highlights: Oil Reform Meets Persistent Production Losses

frictionVectors.title: Upstream Security and Foreign Operators
frictionVectors.details: The state is pursuing higher output and investment through regulatory reform, but theft, pipeline vandalism, and aging infrastructure continue to weaken control over petroleum revenues. International oil companies remain important while divestments shift assets toward less transparent local ownership structures.

frictionVectors.title: Gas, Refining, and Power Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: New refining and gas projects could reduce import dependence, yet unreliable electricity, transport constraints, and financing needs limit national leverage. Foreign lenders, contractors, and technology providers still shape major infrastructure decisions.

highlights: Mineral Hub Ambitions Face Traceability Pressure
Regional Security Leverage Brings External Scrutiny

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Mineral and Security Nexus
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional security posture and alleged links to armed actors in eastern DRC continue to generate diplomatic pressure and scrutiny over mineral supply chains. Sanctions risk, border instability, and contested trade routes could constrain Kigali's resource strategy.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Processing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda is building a reputation in tantalum and other critical-mineral processing, but export markets, certification systems, and capital remain heavily influenced by foreign partners. Its value-addition ambitions therefore coexist with vulnerability to external compliance demands.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea exploration
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is seeking offshore energy investment, but uncertain reserves and limited state capacity leave bargaining power constrained. Any future hydrocarbons deal will face scrutiny over revenue-sharing and environmental safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign partners for ports, connectivity, and public finance. Competition among European, Chinese, and Gulf-linked actors creates leverage without yet producing a dominant external patron.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and gas contract reset
frictionVectors.details: New offshore production gives Dakar greater fiscal room, but the government is pressing for stronger local content, contract transparency, and national control. Disputes with international operators could slow investment if renegotiation becomes unpredictable.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics competition
frictionVectors.details: Dakar's strategic port and transport corridors attract European, Gulf, and Chinese financing. Debt exposure and concession terms remain sensitive as Senegal seeks infrastructure while preserving policy autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Fisheries sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles depends on foreign access arrangements and enforcement partnerships to manage tuna fisheries. The government must balance licensing revenue against concerns that distant-water fleets capture too much value.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic maritime competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China, France, and other partners compete for influence through maritime security, port access, and infrastructure. Victoria has generally preserved room for maneuver, but external financing can narrow that autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Iron ore and mining concentration
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale iron ore and mineral projects provide export potential but leave the state exposed to commodity cycles, operator concentration, and disputes over taxation and local benefits. Weak downstream processing limits domestic value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed port, road, and energy projects are important for growth but can create long-term fiscal and strategic liabilities. Contract transparency and debt sustainability remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime hydrocarbons and security
frictionVectors.details: Somalia is pursuing offshore oil and gas while facing limited enforcement capacity, piracy risks, and contested maritime authority. Foreign exploration and security partnerships could generate revenue but may deepen disputes over ownership and benefit-sharing.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, corridors, and regional rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other actors seek influence through ports, military cooperation, and trade corridors. The Somaliland dispute and tensions over access to the Red Sea complicate Mogadishu's efforts to consolidate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control in strategic minerals
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains regulatory authority over platinum, manganese and other critical minerals, but relies heavily on foreign capital, technology and export markets. Policy uncertainty continues to limit sovereign bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight infrastructure stress
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port bottlenecks constrain mineral beneficiation and exports. State capacity is being supplemented by private operators and external finance, creating sovereignty trade-offs.

highlights: Oil revenue remains the state’s lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil infrastructure and transit dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on pipelines and export routes through Sudan, leaving national revenue exposed to conflict, transit fees and foreign operational control. Production disruptions directly threaten state solvency.

frictionVectors.title: Armed competition around resource zones
frictionVectors.details: Political and local armed actors compete over oil-producing areas and associated revenue flows. External security and commercial partners can gain leverage where domestic institutions remain weak.

frictionVectors.title: Gold networks and external sponsors
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling provide liquidity to armed factions while foreign traders and regional networks capture much of the value. This undermines centralized control over Sudan’s principal monetizable resource.

frictionVectors.title: Ports, pipelines and wartime access
frictionVectors.details: Conflict threatens Red Sea logistics, oil transit and major infrastructure, increasing the influence of neighboring states and outside security actors. Fragmented control makes long-term resource governance increasingly difficult.

highlights: Strategic minerals under tighter state oversight

frictionVectors.title: LNG development and fiscal sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over large offshore gas projects offer major revenue potential but require international capital, technology and export infrastructure. Contract terms and local-content implementation remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals investment pressure
frictionVectors.details: Tanzania is seeking more domestic processing and state participation in mining, while foreign firms retain advantages in finance, technology and marketing. The government’s regulatory posture is improving but remains exposed to investor pressure.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Togo’s strategic port supports regional commerce but depends on foreign shipping, logistics and financing networks. Disruptions or shifts in neighboring markets can quickly reduce national leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector modernization gap
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain strategically important, yet limited processing capacity restricts domestic value capture. External capital and technical expertise are likely to shape future sector development.

frictionVectors.title: EU migration and financing leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU substantial influence over Tunisian policy. Fiscal stress limits Tunis's room to reject external conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Domestic energy vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic production and reliance on Algerian gas expose Tunisia to supply and pricing pressure. Delays in renewable investment and grid reform prolong this vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP sovereignty and environmental dispute
frictionVectors.details: The EACOP project promises export revenue but leaves Uganda dependent on foreign operators, lenders, and transit arrangements through Tanzania. Land acquisition and environmental opposition continue to generate international pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-backed infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed transport and energy projects expand connectivity while increasing repayment and contractor dependence. Kampala is seeking diversified partners but remains exposed to concentrated external financing.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-minerals competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to secure better terms in copper and cobalt. Processing capacity and transport bottlenecks still leave much value captured outside the country.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF oversight stabilize finances but constrain discretionary industrial policy. Reliance on regional rail and port corridors makes mineral exports vulnerable to external infrastructure decisions.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of mineral value chains
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms remain deeply embedded in lithium, platinum, and other mineral operations, while local processing ambitions face financing and power constraints. Export restrictions improve bargaining power but have not yet produced broad domestic beneficiation.

frictionVectors.title: Power and sanctions bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and restricted access to international finance raise operating costs across mining and manufacturing. Harare's dependence on external lenders and politically aligned investors limits its ability to set terms independently.
